Laughter). This question of woman suffrage is almost as old as the hills. The question of woman rights, out of which it grew, dates back to that memorable scene in the garden of Eden. You can follow it down throughout the ages. You can follow it down through the time of Plato down to the days of Montesquieu. Montesquieu believed in the freedom of women, but the kind of freedom the Englishmen believed in for the people of Ireland. They said, build a wall around Ireland and put all the Irish inside and give them all the freedom they want. But that is not the kind of freedom I believe in for women. I have received a large number of letters since this subject was opened up here, since the bill was introduced before, from intelligent and earnest women of this state asking me to give my support to this measure. So far as I can remember I replied to all of those letters and told the writers in substance that I would give careful attention to the arguments pro and con and then would make up my mind and act according as my conscience dictated. I have fulfilled that part of the request, and now I will merely say that in fulfilling my promise made since that time to vote for this bill I do so because I believe there is no such thing as hell.

been packed away in moth balls. So
instructions were issued for all of

same time I saw General King com-

at such a distance that we would
certainly meet opposite the flower
decked sentry. Regulating my voice
so that the sentry would hear me
and the general would not, I called
out frantically. Steele, take that
damned thing off. Take it off,
saying, repeating the command with
appropriate trimmings several times.

parently uncertain whether I want-

of sorrow than of anger and in
few moments the floral decorations
were scattered on the sidewalk.

commanders of the other two regi-
ments, succeeded to the command
of the brigade, but at the same time
retaining command of my own regi-
ment. At the Presidio we had target
practice and many battle exercises
with blank ammunition, and the men
began to get a mild foretaste of
what a battle is like, as the ad-
vancing companies rushed forward
throwing themselves prone at every
halt, their front thick with smoke
while the roar of the old Spring-

Authorities state that if consumers carried the amount of copper now they did 15 or 20 years ago, proportionate to the annual consumption then and now, there would be very little if any visible surplus at present. It is claimed by some of the producing interests that the publication of figures every month showing output, imports, exports and domestic deliveries and supplies on hand, is a severe obstruction to the free and natural conduct of business. Consumers view these figures through magnifying glasses, it is claimed, and are afraid to buy when stocks are large, and that they will be afraid to refrain from buying when stocks again drop to minimum. Thus their action, influenced by the published figures, operates to the detriment of both producers and consumers. When producers want to and need to sell, consumers will not buy; and when producers have little or no copper to sell, consumers buy and bid prices up against one another. It is this view of the situation that causes some prominent interests in the trade to strongly advocate the abolition of the Copper Producers association monthly figures.

The need of a selling agreement between producers is keenly felt especially at the present time, and many consumers as well as producers regret that one cannot be effected legally. It is understood that German consumers, for instance, now buy their copper through central committee, thus taking advantage over American producers that the United States government will not permit the mining interests to meet and resist. The producing interests are of much greater importance to the American people, as only 40 to 45 per cent of our copper is consumed here, the remainder being sold abroad. It is reasonable, therefore, that a protective selling agreement should be permitted, provided it can be conducted on lines that are acceptable to both the manufacturers and the ultimate consumers.

Fluctuations Annoy.

Conditions in the trade are such that violent fluctuations in the price of the metals are more annoying to consumers and work even a greater injury to them than to the producers. While low prices to a certain extent encourage consumption, much more copper would be consumed were prices maintained regularly and steadily around 14 or 15 cents. Compared with the average prices of the other countries with which it competes, copper is well worth 15 cents a pound. If maintained at this price consumption would increase, I relieve, even more rapidly in the future than it did in the past. This would mean fair profit to producers and the proper encouragement of a great American industry.

When general business conditions in this country improve, the copper situation will work out all right however, whether there be a selling agreement or not; but the resumption of a heavy consuming demand cannot fail to force the price up to an abnormal level, even as it did in 1906 and 1907. As the metal market is now regulated, or as it regulates itself, extreme advances cannot be avoided.

The unsettled condition of the metal market and other adverse influences are preventing any active buying of copper. The market continues dull and rather weak. The most discouraging thing about it is the failure of news of important developments at particular properties to be reflected by an increased buying demand for the stock. This shows an entire absence of speculative interest. The delay of the supreme court decisions is not only the chief obstacle to activity in the speculative and investment markets, but it is bringing about business paralysis all over the country. When these decisions are out of the way there is likely to be a general resumption of activity in every direction.

The state of public confidence, often referred to as mere matter of sentiment, is always a vital factor in making for dullness and declining prices, or activity and strength in the stock market. Scores of people have written me recently stating that they are now taking no interest in speculation whatever, but that they are going to hold their stocks until they again sell at former high levels. These letters denote confidence in the future, but not in the present. Otherwise stated, the public is not expecting any improvement in the market immediately, but it firmly believes speculative enthusiasm and investment confidence will return eventually.

Effect of Sentiment.

Day to day traders have been bearish on copper for eight months past. During this period prices have had a considerable recovery, from the low points reached last July, but more recently have been sagging, the price average having been reduced by declines in a certain few.

Los Angeles, Cal. Nov. 10.--"If I
don't live to take care of my baby,
she is my mother's."


This was the message left by Mrs.
Ida Dismukes when she found that
she had but short time to live. It
was written five months before her
death, which occurred Nov. 1. It is
the basis of the defense made in
Judge Wilbur's court yesterday by
her parents, Mr. and Mrs. Draper,
to the petition for the writ of
habeas corpus, made by Samuel A.
Dismukes for the custody of his dear
daughter Dorothy.


Mrs. Dismukes discovered six
months ago that she would soon die.
Last June she wrote the note dispos-
ing of her child. It was the only will
she left. She wanted the baby to re-
main with her mother.


According to the affidavits of the
Drapers, Dismukes neglected his wife
and child for some time prior to his
wife's death. They charge that he
even allowed his wife and baby to
suffer from cold. Her parents took
their daughter and her child to their
own home.


The little girl was ordered before
Judge Wilbur yesterday, but a phy-
sician's certificate showed that she
had whooping cough and it would
have been dangerous to bring her to
court.


The testimony before Judge Wilbur
showed that the fight for custody of
the child started the day her mother
was buried. The father's sister, after
the funeral, demanded that the Dra-
pers give her the child. The grand-
parents protested and showed the
note left by their daughter.


The interview between Miss Merle
Dismukes and the Drapers at the
time resulted in Dismukes filing a
petition for writ of habeas corpus.
The Drapers, represented by Walter
V. Dysert, filed another petition with
the county clerk, asking to be ap-
pointed her guardian.


Judge Wilbur continued the case
until next Friday, ruling that little
Dorothy remain with her mother's
parents until the case is settled.
Though the law provides that the
father is the natural guardian of the
child, the juvenile court has the power
to place her with others, and Judge
Wilbur will decide this matter.
